Electrooculography provides a practical way to use eye activity as an input signal for computer interaction.
This paper describes a low-cost EOG-based prototype developed to recognize four ocular states: neutral
gaze, upward eye movement, downward eye movement, and blinking. The hardware consists of a BioAmp
EXG Pill connected to an ESP32 microcontroller. Vertical EOG is recorded using electrodes positioned above
and below the right eye, while the ESP32 samples the signal at 500 Hz, performs initial filtering, and
transmits the processed values to a computer.
The available dataset contains 64,000 samples collected across 160 trials, with 40 trials for each class. Every
trial lasts 0.8 s and contains 400 samples. A set of 28 han

The available dataset contains 64,000 samples collected across 160 trials, with 40 trials for each class. Every
trial lasts 0.8 s and contains 400 samples. A set of 28 handcrafted features was extracted from each trial,
covering statistical properties, signal trend, peak behavior, spectral content, and Hjorth mobility. Random
Forest, Gradient Boosting, and radial-basis-function Support Vector Machine classifiers were evaluated.
The original implementation used heavily overlapping windows and reported 89.27% five-fold cross-
validation accuracy and 91.14% hold-out accuracy with Gradient Boosting. Since neighboring windows
shared 87.5% of their samples, this evaluation could overestimate generalization. To obtain a stricter
estimate from the same data, the 160 acquisition trials were reconstructed and evaluated directly as
independent examples. Under five-fold stratified trial-level cross-validation, Random Forest achieved the
highest mean accuracy of 78.75%

independent examples. Under five-fold stratified trial-level cross-validation, Random Forest achieved the
highest mean accuracy of 78.75% ± 10.90%, with a mean macro F1-score of 78.68% ± 10.80%. Blink and
neutral trials were recognized more reliably than the two directional classes, while most directional errors
occurred between upward and downward movements.
The classifier was also integrated into a real-time control program. Upward and downward predictions
move the cursor vertically, while a double blink is mapped to a mouse click. Prediction confidence, short-
term voting, and an action cooldown are used to reduce unstable commands. The results show that a
relatively inexpensive EOG setup can support a functioning machine-learning-based interaction prototype.
At the same time, the current dataset does not contain participant identifiers, so subject-independent
performance cannot be assessed.

Abstract

1. Introduction
Most computer interfaces assume that a user can interact physically with a mouse, keyboard, touchscreen,
or controller. That assumption does not always hold. Hands-free interaction can be useful in assistive
systems, constrained working environments, and experimental human–machine interfaces. One way to
create such an interface is to use physiological signals as an additional input channel.
Brain–computer interface research has established a general processing chain in which physiological
activity is acquired, processed, classified, and converted into commands for an external system [Wolpaw et
al., 2002]. In this context, electroencephalography and electrooculography should be treated differently.
EEG measures electrical activity associated with the brain, while EOG reflects changes in the electrical field
around the eye caused by ocular movement. The project described here used both ideas at prototype level,
but the EOG component is the part for which a complete datase

s changes in the electrical field
around the eye caused by ocular movement. The project described here used both ideas at prototype level,
but the EOG component is the part for which a complete dataset, training pipeline, trained model, and
evaluation report are available. The quantitative study therefore focuses on EOG.
The electrical potential between the front and back of the eye changes relative to electrodes placed around
the eye as gaze direction changes. This makes EOG suitable for detecting intentional eye movements and
blinking [Chang, 2019]. Previous studies have used EOG for cursor control, virtual keyboards, mobility
systems, communication aids, and other hands-free interfaces [Chang, 2019; Belkhiria et al., 2022].
EOG also comes with practical difficulties. The recorded signal can drift over time, change with electrode
placement, pick up muscle and electrical interference, and vary between sessions and users. Blinks may be
intentional or involuntary, and small directional

can drift over time, change with electrode
placement, pick up muscle and electrical interference, and vary between sessions and users. Blinks may be
intentional or involuntary, and small directional movements can be difficult to separate reliably. For these
reasons, a useful EOG system requires more than simple signal acquisition. The processing and evaluation
strategy matters as much as the hardware.
Several previous systems have used conventional machine-learning methods for this purpose. Ang et al.
[2015] demonstrated cursor control using a wearable single-channel EOG interface based on blink patterns.
Martínez-Cerveró et al. [2020] presented an open EOG platform for classifying directional eye movements.
Hernández Pérez et al. [2023] evaluated wavelet-based EOG features with several supervised classifiers.
The present work explores a smaller command vocabulary using inexpensive hardware. The system
recognizes Neutral, Up, Down, and Blink states from vertical EOG recordings and map

3
The work does not introduce a new classifier or a new EOG sensing principle. Its value lies in the complete
low-cost pipeline and in the evaluation of how well that pipeline performs on the collected data.
EOG measures changes in the electrical potential around the eye as the eye moves. A common engineering
approximation treats the eye as an electrical dipole, with the corneal side relatively positive compared with
the retinal side [Chang, 2019]. When the direction of gaze changes, the voltage measured by nearby
electrodes also changes.
Electrode position determines which movements can be measured most directly. Electrodes placed to the left
and right of the eyes are commonly used for horizontal movement. Electrodes placed above and below an
eye are suitable for vertical movement and also capture strong responses during blinking.
Chang [2019] reviewed the use of EOG in human–computer interaction, including cursor, keyboard,
communication, and mobility applications. Belkhiria et al. [

Chang [2019] reviewed the use of EOG in human–computer interaction, including cursor, keyboard,
communication, and mobility applications. Belkhiria et al. [2022] reviewed EOG-HCI work published over two
decades and described acquisition, preprocessing, feature extraction, classification, and command
translation as recurring components of these systems.
The architecture used in this project follows the same general idea, although the implementation is
intentionally small and low-cost.
2.2 EOG for Cursor Control
Cursor control is a natural EOG application because directional movement can be translated into navigation
and blinking can be translated into a selection command.
Ang et al. [2015] developed a wearable single-channel EOG interface that used blink patterns for cursor
operation. Martínez-Cerveró et al. [2020] investigated directional EOG classification using an open software/
hardware platform and supervised learning.

These studies are relevant to the present work because they show that a limited set of ocular gestures can be
converted into practical computer commands. However, direct comparison of accuracy values would be
misleading because the hardware, classes, participants, features, and validation procedures differ.
2.3 Conventional Classifiers for EOG
The current project compares three established models rather than introducing a new learning algorithm.
Random Forest combines multiple decision trees and aggregates their predictions [Breiman, 2001]. It is
useful for nonlinear relationships and mixed feature types.

2.4 Feature Representation
A single amplitude threshold does not capture every property of an EOG waveform. The current system
therefore combines several kinds of information: amplitude statistics, waveform slope, zero crossings, peak
structure, temporal changes, spectral components, and Hjorth mobility.
Hjorth mobility was introduced as a time-domain descriptor for electrophysiological signals [Hjorth, 1970].
In this work it is used simply as another measure of waveform behavior, without assigning a physiological
interpretation to it.

12.5 Double Blink
A blink is stored temporarily.
If a second blink is detected within 700 ms of the first, the program sends a mouse click.
Thus, the machine-learning model identifies individual blink events, while the interface logic determines
whether those events form a double blink.
The most important result is not simply the highest accuracy value. The comparison between the two
evaluation strategies gives a more useful picture of the system.
The original pipeline reported 91.14% hold-out accuracy, but those windows overlapped by 87.5%. Two
neighboring windows could therefore contain mostly the same signal.

When complete acquisition trials were treated as the evaluation units, the best mean accuracy fell to
78.75%.
That lower result is less visually impressive, but it is more informative. It suggests that the original
overlapping-window experiment was easier than classifying separate recorded trials.
The change in model ranking is also worth noting. Gradient Boosting was strongest in the original pipeline,
whereas Random Forest performed better under the trial-level analysis. This does not establish that
Random Forest is generally better for EOG. It simply shows that the preferred model can depend on how
the data is divided.
The class results also show that all four classes were not equally difficult. Neutral and Blink were classified
more reliably, while Up and Down produced more mutual errors.
This is plausible given that both directional

lso show that all four classes were not equally difficult. Neutral and Blink were classified
more reliably, while Up and Down produced more mutual errors.
This is plausible given that both directional states were recorded using the same vertical electrode pair.
However, the dataset does not allow the cause of those errors to be isolated. They may reflect differences in
movement timing, electrode contact, signal variability, preprocessing, or limitations of the feature
representation.
The feature-group analysis gives a similar caution. The full 28-feature vector performed best, but the
advantage over the statistical and frequency-only groups was modest. The result supports using mixed
features in this dataset, but it does not establish an optimal feature set.
The real-time control layer is also important because a classification model by itself is not a complete
interface. A single false prediction can immediately become an unwanted cursor movement. For this
reason, the implementation u

also important because a classification model by itself is not a complete
interface. A single false prediction can immediately become an unwanted cursor movement. For this
reason, the implementation uses a confidence threshold, a short voting buffer, and an action cooldown.
These mechanisms reduce unstable commands, although they may also increase effective response time.
Because end-to-end latency was not measured, the current study does not claim a specific interaction
speed.
Overall, the prototype demonstrates that the acquired EOG signal contains enough information to support
a small four-class control vocabulary. The remaining question is how well the same approach would work
across different people and recording sessions, which cannot be answered from the current dataset.

15.6 Difference Between Offline and Real-Time Filtering
The training code uses forward-backward filtering, while the online controller uses causal streaming
filtering.
The two approaches do not produce perfectly identical waveforms.
A later version should use the same causal preprocessing during both training and deployment.
15.7 End-to-End Latency Was Not Recorded
The 100 ms prediction-update interval is determined by the 50-sample step size.
It does not include the full delay introduced by signal acquisition, window formation, filtering, feature
extraction, classification, voting, cooldown logic, and cursor execution.
No measured end-to-end latency is available.

15.8 No Controlled User Study
The prototype was used as a working interface, but no structured study measured command success, false
activations, click success, or task-completion time.
The present results should therefore be interpreted as classifier and implementation results rather than a
full usability evaluation.

Neutral gaze and blinking were classified more reliably than the two directional movements, while the

The same EOG classes were connected to a real-time cursor-control program. Up and Down predictions
produced vertical movement, and two detected blinks within 700 ms produced a mouse click. Confidence
filtering, short-term voting, and an action cooldown were used to reduce unstable commands.
The results support the feasibility of the current prototype, but they should not be treated as evidence of
user-independent assistive performance. The next meaningful improvement is a multi-participant dataset
with explicit participant and trial identifiers, followed by subject-independent evaluation.
